strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: reducing the substantial inference and memory costs of billion-parameter 3D reconstruction transformers. The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/72ea8afc66834a63bda6391b2cb34652/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed framework is coherent: Hadamard rotation, channel smoothing, fine-grained quantization, and calibration-set construction target plausible failure modes of VGGT quantization.

The reported W4A4 results are promising and substantially outperform the adapted generic PTQ baselines, particularly for camera pose estimation on Co3Dv2. Cross-dataset point-map evaluation on DTU provides some evidence of generalization.
The experiments cover several bit widths, multiple established baselines, component ablations, five-seed sampling experiments, calibration overhead, memory consumption, and measured latency.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 and its proof are not sound. The proof simply asserts that the expected subregions have equal scale, which does not follow from the premises. Moreover, the theorem advocates sampling proportional to region prevalence, whereas the method appears to take equal samples from K-means clusters. Maximum entropy over arbitrarily defined clusters does not establish that the resulting set best represents the data distribution or minimizes quantization error.

The methodological novelty is limited. DSFQ primarily composes established Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, and fine-grained activation quantization; NFDS combines conventional outlier filtering and K-means sampling. The paper does not clearly isolate a sufficiently novel technical principle beyond tailoring these components to VGGT.

Evaluation is restricted to one backbone, two datasets, and two of VGGT's several tasks. There is no evidence on depth estimation, tracking, other visual-geometry foundation models, varying calibration domains, or meaningfully different sequence lengths beyond 10 and 20 frames. This makes the broader claims about VGGTs and large 3D models insufficiently supported.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract contains an empty code-release statement, while the reproducibility section promises code only after publication. Important details are missing, including the exact layers and operators quantized, treatment of nonlinearities and task heads, inference hardware and software stack, integer kernels and packing scheme, batch size, input resolution, baseline tuning budgets, and precise latency measurement protocol.

Baseline fairness is unclear. The manuscript says comparative results are sourced from public literature even though the reported VGGT settings appear specialized, and it does not explain how generic baselines were adapted or tuned. QuantVGGT also benefits from its custom calibration selection, but it is unclear whether baselines received comparably optimized calibration data and budgets.

Several technical descriptions are imprecise. A matrix with entries in {-1,+1} cannot simultaneously satisfy H^T H = I without normalization; channel-scale indexing and statistics are underspecified; the threshold T is described as a percentile but later set to 0.2 without clarification; and the claim that dynamic token-wise activation quantization adds essentially no cost lacks implementation evidence.

Most accuracy results are single-number estimates without uncertainty or significance analysis. The five-seed study covers only the sampling ablation, so small W8A8 gains over full precision or competing methods cannot be judged reliably.

The ethics statement categorically claims that 3D reconstruction creates no ethics-related risks, overlooking plausible privacy and surveillance applications. Even if the incremental quantization method creates limited new risk, the statement should acknowledge downstream misuse and deployment considerations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant deployment problem: low-bit post-training quantization of the 1.2B-parameter VGGT model, an important but relatively unexplored setting.

The reported W4A4 results are substantial. On Co3Dv2, QuantVGGT improves AUC@30 from QuaRot's 81.8 to 86.9 for 10 frames, while on DTU it improves mean accuracy error from 1.593 to 1.282. Evaluation includes W4A4, W6A6, and W8A8 settings and both in-domain and cross-dataset tasks.

The component and efficiency studies are useful: rotation, smoothing, quantization granularity, filtering, clustering, random-seed variability, memory, calibration cost, and latency are considered. The claimed 3.65x memory reduction and 2.49x latency improvement would be practically valuable if reproduced.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 and its proof are technically invalid. The proof treats E(X) as a sample space, asserts without justification that all region volumes become equal after expectation, and proves only that entropy over arbitrary region assignments is maximized by a uniform distribution. This neither establishes the theorem's claimed volume-proportional sampling result nor justifies uniform sampling from K-means clusters. Indeed, uniform sampling per cluster generally oversamples small clusters rather than preserving their prevalence.

The main accuracy-retention claim is misleading. The cited 98% retention uses only the lenient AUC@30 metric: at W4A4, AUC@3 falls from 54.9 to 43.6 for 10 frames and from 56.9 to 45.1 for 20 frames, retaining only about 79%. Thus the broad claim of maintaining reconstruction accuracy above 98% is not supported across the reported metrics.

Methodological novelty is limited. DSFQ largely composes established Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, and fine-grained dynamic quantization. NFDS combines outlier rejection and K-means sampling. The manuscript does not establish sufficiently clearly which aspects constitute a nontrivial advance beyond this combination of known techniques.

There are technical imprecisions in the method. In particular, a matrix with entries in {-1,+1} cannot satisfy H^T H=I without normalization. The motivation for deleting rare activation outliers also conflicts with the stated objective of approximating the true deployment distribution and could impair tail-case robustness.

The evaluation is too narrow for the broad VGGT claims: only one model is studied, with two datasets and two of VGGT's several output tasks. There is no evaluation of depth estimation or point tracking, no second architecture, and little analysis of different scene domains, sequence lengths beyond 10/20 frames, calibration-set sizes, or sensitivity to K, T, and alpha.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The paper does not give enough implementation and tuning details for adapting BRECQ, QDrop, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, and DopQ-ViT to VGGT. The reproducibility statement confusingly says comparative results are sourced from public literature even though the paper presents VGGT-specific comparisons, and the promised code is not presently available.

The hardware claims omit essential information such as the inference GPU, batch size, kernels/backend, timing protocol, warm-up, and whether latency is end-to-end. Consequently, the central 2.5x real-hardware speedup cannot be independently interpreted or reproduced.

Some ablations remain confounded or unclear: the primary DSFQ comparison combines rotation, smoothing, and granularity; the relationship between the Base/Naive PTQ values across Tables 3 and 7 is unexplained; and the modest NFDS gain is based on only five seeds without significance testing. Overall, the promising empirical results do not overcome the invalid theoretical justification, overstated claim, limited novelty, and incomplete reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely, practically important problem: deploying the 1.2B-parameter VGGT through post-training quantization. The diagnosis of special-token activation outliers and unstable multi-view calibration is well motivated and specific to this model family.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and computationally practical. Combining Hadamard rotation, post-rotation channel smoothing, fine-grained quantization, outlier filtering, and frame-aware calibration sampling is sensible.

The W4A4 results are compelling: on Co3Dv2, QuantVGGT reaches AUC@30 of 86.9/88.2 for 10/20 frames, substantially exceeding QuaRot's 81.8/81.6; on DTU, its accuracy error of 1.282 is much closer to the FP16 value of 1.185 than competing PTQ methods.

The evaluation includes diverse generic baselines, W4A4/W6A6/W8A8 settings, cross-dataset transfer from Co3Dv2 calibration to DTU evaluation, component ablations, five-seed sampling experiments, calibration costs, and measured latency and memory improvements.

The reported 3.65x memory reduction and 2.49x latency improvement at W4A4, with only a small overhead relative to naive quantization, make the contribution relevant beyond accuracy alone. weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 is not technically justified. The proof assumes without support that the expected subregions have equal scales, reduces the objective to ordinary entropy maximization, and consequently establishes uniform probabilities—not the stated proportional-to-scale result for unequal regions. The subsequent recommendation to sample uniformly across K-means clusters can also overrepresent small clusters and conflicts with the stated proportional-sampling principle.

Methodological novelty is moderate. DSFQ largely composes established Hadamard rotation and SmoothQuant-style scaling, while NFDS combines standardized outlier filtering with K-means sampling. The VGGT-specific adaptation and empirical gains are valuable, but the paper overstates the conceptual novelty and theoretical foundation.

The scope is narrow for claims about VGGTs or large-scale 3D transformers: all experiments use a single VGGT-1B checkpoint, with only camera pose on Co3Dv2 and point-map estimation on DTU. Depth estimation, tracking, additional datasets, other model variants, and broader scene distributions are not evaluated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Code is only promised after publication, and important details are missing or ambiguous: precisely which layers and operations are quantized or retained in floating point, baseline-specific tuning, calibration-pool construction, clustering initialization, inference hardware, kernel implementation, warm-up and timing protocol, batch size, and treatment of attention nonlinearities. The statement that comparison results are sourced from public literature is also difficult to reconcile with this novel VGGT evaluation and needs clarification.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. It is unclear whether every baseline receives the same block-wise reconstruction procedure, dynamic token-wise granularity, calibration budget, and comparable hyperparameter tuning. Since these choices provide large gains by themselves, unequal treatment could materially affect the headline margins.

Most headline results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics; only the sampling ablation reports five seeds. Hyperparameter sensitivity for the filtering threshold, number of clusters, calibration-set size, and smoothing coefficient is absent.

The Hadamard presentation contains technical imprecision: a matrix with entries in {-1,+1} cannot simultaneously satisfy H^T H=I without normalization. More broadly, the claimed central-limit behavior is presented as a lemma without suitable conditions.

The ethics statement's categorical claim of no risk is too strong. Making large-scale 3D reconstruction cheaper can facilitate privacy-invasive mapping or surveillance, so deployment-related dual-use risks merit at least brief discussion. Overall, the strong empirical evidence makes the paper promising, but the invalid theorem and evaluation/reproducibility gaps leave it marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: deploying billion-parameter visual-geometry transformers using low-bit post-training quantization.

QuantVGGT achieves strong W4A4 results relative to numerous generic PTQ baselines. The evaluation covers camera pose estimation, point-map estimation, point-cloud reconstruction, multiple sequence lengths, four datasets, and an additional Fast3R backbone.

The component studies are reasonably extensive, covering rotation and smoothing order, activation granularity, calibration sampling, hyperparameter sensitivity, calibration cost, memory, and hardware latency.
The reported deployment gains are substantial: approximately 3.65x memory reduction and 2.49x latency improvement on an RTX 4090, with only a modest degradation on several reconstruction metrics.
The paper is well organized, visually polished, and motivates the special-token activation outliers clearly.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for NFDS is unsound. Theorem 3.2 claims that sampling proportional to region volume maximizes entropy, whereas entropy is maximized by a uniform distribution over regions. Its proof simply assumes equal expected region volumes without justification. Moreover, the implemented equal-per-cluster sampling does not approximate proportional sampling unless clusters have equal mass. Thus, the theorem does not support the proposed procedure.

The methodological novelty is limited. DSFQ principally composes established Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, and token-wise activation quantization; NFDS combines conventional outlier filtering and K-means sampling. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from a careful engineering integration of known techniques.

Several central claims are overstated. W4A4 preserves about 98% only for the relatively saturated AUC@30 metric, while AUC@3 falls from 54.9 to 43.6, roughly 79% retention. Statements such as 'without compromising visual quality' and 'nearly lossless' are therefore not uniformly supported.

Reproducibility and baseline fairness are insufficient. The code-release link is blank and the reproducibility statement only promises code after publication. Important details such as which layers remain unquantized, baseline adaptation and tuning, evaluation sample counts, input resolution, latency protocol, and exact memory measurement are missing. The assertion that comparative results come from public literature is also unclear because the cited generic methods did not originally report VGGT results.

The efficiency evidence needs clearer accounting. Quantization does not ordinarily reduce mathematical FLOPs, yet Table 7 reports a reduction from 5.84T to 1.40T without defining a bit-adjusted operation metric. End-to-end latency is presented mainly as normalized speedup, without uncertainty, warm-up/repetition details, or comparisons on additional hardware.

NFDS provides a relatively small gain compared with the architecture changes, and evidence that filtering does not remove important rare geometry modes is limited. The 'extreme case' experiment improves AUC@30 by only 0.2 over random sampling and does not establish broad robustness.

The analysis attributes outlier behavior to special tokens mostly through qualitative plots; targeted interventions such as quantizing special and image tokens separately, removing or retaining special tokens at higher precision, or reporting per-token quantization error would more directly validate the claimed mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem: efficient deployment of billion-parameter visual-geometry transformers.

The reported W4A4 results are substantial. QuantVGGT consistently outperforms generic PTQ baselines across camera-pose, point-map, and point-cloud evaluations, while retaining much of the full-precision accuracy.
The experiments include multiple datasets, two reconstruction architectures, component and hyperparameter ablations, five-seed calibration-sampling results, and measurements on an RTX 4090.
The combination of rotation, channel smoothing, fine-grained activation quantization, and calibration-set construction is clearly motivated by observed activation behavior.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 and its proof are invalid. The proof simply asserts that all expected region volumes are equal, without justification, and then proves only the standard fact that a uniform categorical distribution maximizes entropy. This does not establish the theorem's claimed proportional-to-volume sampling rule. Moreover, uniform sampling from each K-means cluster generally does not reproduce the population distribution unless clusters have equal mass.

The technical novelty is limited. DSFQ largely combines established Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, and token-wise dynamic quantization. NFDS combines outlier filtering and K-means sampling. The paper does not sharply distinguish the new technical insight from this composition of existing mechanisms.

The empirical attribution is incomplete. Table 4 changes rotation, smoothing order, and quantization granularity together, so it does not isolate how much of the improvement comes from the proposed dual smoothing versus the strong dynamic token-wise quantization choice, which Table 8 itself shows contributes a large gain.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not provide implementation details, tuning budgets, calibration choices, or per-baseline adaptations needed to verify that methods originating in LLMs and 2D vision were compared fairly on VGGT. The reproducibility statement ambiguously says comparative results are sourced from public literature despite presenting this as the first VGGT PTQ study.

The code-release claim is inconsistent: the abstract ends with an incomplete 'Our code is released in' statement, whereas the reproducibility section promises release only after publication. No usable repository or complete reproducibility package is provided.

The efficiency evidence lacks essential measurement details such as batch size, resolution, warm-up, number of timed runs, variance, whether preprocessing and dynamic-scale computation are included, and whether latency is end-to-end. Consequently, the headline 2.5x speedup is difficult to validate.

Several broad claims are stronger than the evidence. The work studies one principal 1.2B model, with only a limited secondary Fast3R experiment, yet repeatedly claims generality to VGGTs or large 3D models. The ethics statement also dismisses all risk without considering privacy or surveillance implications of efficient 3D reconstruction.

Overall, the strong reported results are promising, but the invalid theoretical component, incremental methodological contribution, unclear baseline protocol, and incomplete reproducibility are major issues at a top-tier acceptance bar. strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: low-bit post-training quantization of billion-parameter visual-geometry transformers, a setting that is considerably less explored than language and 2D vision models.

The proposed framework is well motivated by empirical observations about special-token outliers and unstable multi-view calibration. Combining Hadamard rotation, post-rotation channel smoothing, fine-grained quantization, and frame-aware calibration is technically sensible.

The W4A4 results are strong. QuantVGGT substantially outperforms numerous generic PTQ baselines on CO3Dv2 and DTU, remains close to full precision on 7-Scenes and NRGBD, and transfers successfully to Fast3R.
The evaluation covers camera pose estimation, point-map estimation, and point-cloud reconstruction, including cross-dataset calibration/generalization and 10- versus 20-frame inputs.

Ablations separately study rotation, smoothing order, quantization granularity, outlier filtering, clustering, sample size, and key hyperparameters. Results over five sampling seeds support the claim that NFDS improves calibration stability.

The paper reports deployment-oriented measurements on an RTX 4090 using low-bit CUTLASS kernels, with approximately 2.5x latency improvement and 3.65x memory reduction. Calibration costs are also reported and appear practical.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful qualitative reconstructions, sensitivity experiments, an ethics statement, and extensive supplementary analysis.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.2 and its proof are not technically sound as written. The proof asserts without justification that all expected subregions have equal scale, then merely derives the standard result that entropy is maximized by a uniform distribution. This neither proves the stated proportional-to-volume sampling claim nor establishes that uniform sampling from K-means clusters approximates the target data distribution. The theoretical framing should be removed or substantially corrected.

The main architectural idea has limited conceptual novelty: DSFQ largely composes established Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, and fine-grained quantization. The VGGT-specific diagnosis and effective integration are valuable, but the paper sometimes overstates the methodological novelty.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract contains an unfinished code-release sentence, code is promised only after publication, and several important implementation details are underspecified, including precisely which layers and nonlinear operations are quantized, baseline adaptation/tuning, kernel configuration, batch size, and absolute latency.

The efficiency evidence needs more careful presentation. Only relative latency is reported, and the comparison lacks wall-clock measurements against optimized FP16 and alternative quantization implementations across hardware. Table 7 describes bit-width-induced reductions as reduced FLOPs, although quantization changes operation precision rather than the mathematical FLOP count.

The NFDS rationale is not fully validated. Filtering statistically unusual scenes could discard legitimate rare modes, and evaluation is limited to datasets broadly similar to the calibration domain. The reported 'extreme-case' experiment shows only a small gain over random sampling and does not establish robustness on rare but valid geometries.

Some experimental reporting is inconsistent or insufficiently controlled: full-precision CO3Dv2 numbers differ across tables because different subsets appear to be used; uncertainty is reported for the sampling ablation but not for the main benchmarks; and it is unclear whether every baseline received equally optimized calibration data and implementation effort.

The claimed maintenance of more than 98% of full-precision performance relies mainly on AUC@30, while stricter pose thresholds exhibit noticeably larger losses—for example, W4A4 AUC@3 decreases from 54.9 to 43.6. The abstract should qualify this headline rather than imply near-lossless accuracy across metrics.

The ethics discussion is too categorical in claiming no risks. Efficient 3D reconstruction can have privacy or surveillance applications, so a brief acknowledgment of downstream misuse and dataset considerations would be more appropriate.
